items.title: Twenty Marks, Five Causes: Walking the Full Path to Breakthrough

items.zh: 謂於空、無願、無相加行中，於隨入作意微細現行，有間無間隨轉我慢俱行心相能障現觀作意，正通達故。既通達已；於作意俱行心任運轉中，能善棄捨，令無間滅。依無間滅心，由新所起作意，以無常等行如實思惟。由此作意修習、多修習故，所緣能緣平等平等智生。彼於爾時，能障現觀我慢亂心便永斷滅，證得心一境性。便自思惟：我已證得心一境性，如實了知。
items.en: In the preparatory practice of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, a subtle mental state bound up with self-conceit arises — with or without interruption — following along with the attention that enters those gates, and it can obstruct the very attention needed for breakthrough realisation; by genuinely penetrating it, [this obstacle is overcome]. Having penetrated it, in the mind's spontaneous flow together with that attention, one skilfully lets it go, causing it to cease without interruption. Resting on this mind of uninterrupted cessation, through newly arisen attention, one truly contemplates through the practice of impermanence and the rest. Through cultivating — and repeatedly cultivating — this attention, the wisdom of object and subject as utterly equal arises. At that time, the confused mind of self-conceit that obstructs direct realisation is permanently cut off, and one attains one-pointedness of mind. One then reflects: "I have attained one-pointedness of mind," and knows this as it truly is.

items.zh: 當知是名由通達作意故，入諦現觀。
items.en: It should be understood that this is called entering direct realisation of the truths through penetrating attention.

items.title: Causes Two Through Five: Concentration, Object, Resources, and Means

items.zh: 又若先以世間道得三摩地，亦得圓滿，亦得自在。彼或於入三摩地相，謂由此故入三摩地；或於住三摩地相，謂由此故住三摩地；或於出三摩地相，謂由此故出三摩地；於此諸相作意思惟，安住其心，入諦現觀。若得三摩地，而未圓滿，亦未自在。彼或思惟止相、或思惟舉相、或思惟捨相，安住其心，入諦現觀。如是當知由所依故，其心安住。又有二法，於修現觀極為障礙。何等為二？一、不正尋思所作擾亂，心不安靜；二、於所知事其心顛倒。為欲對治如是障礙，當知有二種於所緣境安住其心。謂為對治第一障故，修阿那波那念；為對治第二障故，修諸念住。如是當知由入境界門故，其心安住。又於妙五欲樂習近者，於聖法毘奈耶，非所行處。若於隨宜所得衣服、飲食、諸坐臥具，便生喜足；隨所獲得利養恭敬，制伏其心。謂依妙五欲，不由所得利養恭敬，心便堅住；由此因緣，遠離一切非所行處。既遠離已，依諸念住樂斷樂修。於晝夜分，時時觀察自他所有衰盛等事，心生厭患。又復修習佛隨念等，令心清淨。又復安住諸聖種中。如是當知由資糧故，其心安住。此依最勝資糧道說。又彼如是資糧住已，為修相應作意加行，故有二種加行方便。何等為二？一、自於契經阿毘達磨，讀誦受持，修正作意，於蘊等事令極善巧。二、依他師教，所謂大師、鄔波柁耶、阿遮利耶。於時時間，教授教誡，攝受依止。又正加行作意思惟，當知是名第三方便。此正加行作意思惟，名正加行。此中義者，謂尸羅淨所有作意，名正加行作意思惟。
items.en: Again, if one has already attained concentration by a mundane path, whether fully perfected and mastered — steadying the mind through the marks of entering concentration, of abiding in concentration, and of emerging from concentration — one enters the direct realisation of the truths. If concentration is attained but not yet perfected or mastered, one steadies the mind instead through the marks of calming, of uplifting, and of equanimity, and so enters the direct realisation of the truths. There are, further, two things that greatly obstruct the cultivation of direct realisation: disturbance caused by improper reflection, leaving the mind unsettled; and a mind inverted regarding what should be known. …To counter the first obstruction, one cultivates mindfulness of the breath; to counter the second, one cultivates the applications of mindfulness. Again, whoever grows habituated to the pleasures of the fine five sense-desires has strayed from the domain proper to the noble Dharma and discipline. …Having become free of this, resting on the applications of mindfulness, one delights in relinquishing and delights in cultivating. …One further cultivates recollection of the Buddha and the rest, purifying the mind. One further abides within the noble lineages. …One reads, recites, and upholds the discourses and the treatises oneself, cultivating correct attention until fully skilled regarding the aggregates and the rest. …One relies on a teacher's instruction — the Great Teacher [the Buddha], a preceptor, an instructor — receiving, from time to time, their teaching and admonition, taking refuge in their guidance. And correctly applying attention itself should be known as the third means. …This means that attention devoted to the purity of moral discipline is called correctly applying attention.

items.zh: 彼自思惟尸羅清淨，故無悔惱；無悔惱故，便生歡喜；廣說乃至心入正定。是故宣說此正加行作意思惟，名心住方便。由如是方便故，心速安住。
items.en: One reflects that one's moral discipline is pure, and therefore one has no remorse; because one has no remorse, gladness arises; and so on in full, up to the mind entering right concentration. This is why it is said that this applying of attention and reflection in correct practice is called the means of settling the mind. By such means, the mind swiftly becomes settled.

items.title: Section: The Twenty Marks Complete — Entering the Direct Realisation of the Noble Truths

items.zh: 彼於爾時，由此五因二十種相攝持其心，於愛盡寂滅涅槃界中，令善安住，無復退轉，心無驚怖。謂我我今者何所在耶？當於如是心安住時，應知已名入諦現觀。如是名入聖諦現觀。又此聖諦現觀義，廣說應知。謂心厭患相有二十種，心安住相亦二十種。除此更無若過若增。
items.en: At that time, holding the mind by these five causes and twenty marks, one dwells well, without further regression, within the realm of nirvāṇa — the peace of exhausted craving — the mind free of alarm, no longer wondering, "Where, now, has my self gone?" When the mind abides in this way, this should be known as entering the direct realisation of the truths. This is called entering the direct realisation of the noble truths. This meaning of entering the direct realisation of the noble truths should, in full, be understood thus: the marks of the mind's revulsion number twenty, and the marks of the mind's abiding likewise number twenty. Beyond these, there is nothing further to exceed them, and nothing further to add.

blocks.text: The five causes are explained in reverse order, ending in the moment of breakthrough: the direct realisation of the noble truths, that is, stream-entry. Ru-Yi translates most of today's text.

As one attends through the gates of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, "a subtle mental state bound up with self-conceit arises", sometimes interrupted, sometimes not. One sees through even that. Master Cháng Bǎi: not only what is known is impermanent and selfless, but the knowing mind too. One who attains the path knows it "as one knows whether water one drinks is warm or cold", needing no one's confirmation.

The **basis** is perfected and mastered concentration, steadied through the signs of entering, abiding, and emerging. The **object** is the four truths. The **provisions** counter two problems: disturbance from improper reflection, and inverted understanding of what is to be known. The **means** is a teacher: ideally the Buddha, or one's preceptor and instructor. Master Cháng Bǎi explains the upādhyāya and ācārya.

At the edge of realisation the old fear may arise: "Where, now, has my self gone?" Venerable Miào Jìng: "where am I? I fear I no longer exist." The practitioner who has prepared well does not draw back. With direct realisation of the truths, stream-entry is attained, and nirvāṇa is, in part, realised. Venerable Miào Jìng: this is the state of stream-entry.

The detail here is striking: the treatise expects fear at the threshold of insight into non-self, and names it. The preparation of the whole stage, revulsion towards one's own situation and a clear view of the goal, exists partly so that this fear does not win.

quiz.q: In the preparatory practice of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, what obstructs the attention needed for breakthrough?
options: a subtle mental state bound up with self-conceit that follows along, with or without interruption
quiz.why: "A subtle mental state bound up with self-conceit arises — with or without interruption — following along with the attention that enters those gates, and it can obstruct the very attention needed for breakthrough." Master Cháng Bǎi: the habit of discriminating self and other is so deeply rooted that even just before attaining the path, a trace of conceit arises and obstructs it.

quiz.q: How do the two masters explain "the wisdom of object and subject as utterly equal"?
options: the object is the Buddha, the subject me
the object is impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless — and so is the cognizing mind; the two are equal
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: what is cognized is impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless, and the cognizing mind is likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless — object and subject utterly equal. Venerable Miào Jìng: the object is impermanent and selfless, and the cognizing wisdom too is impermanent, selfless, and of the nature of quiescence.

quiz.q: After attaining one-pointedness, one "reflects… and knows this as it truly is." How does Master Cháng Bǎi describe it?
options: like drinking water, one knows its warmth oneself — no one else need confirm it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: one who has attained the noble path knows it as one knows whether water one drinks is warm or cold — no one else's confirmation is needed.

quiz.q: For one who attained concentration by a mundane path, how does the treatise say one steadies the mind to enter direct realisation, depending on one's level?
options: the perfected and mastered use the marks of entering, abiding, and emerging; those not yet perfected use calming, uplifting, and equanimity
quiz.why: One whose concentration is perfected and mastered steadies the mind through the marks of entering, abiding, and emerging; "if concentration is attained but not yet perfected or mastered, one steadies the mind instead through the marks of calming, of uplifting, and of equanimity." Master Cháng Bǎi: those who have only access concentration steady the mind by mastering calming, uplifting, and equanimity.

quiz.q: Which two things does the treatise say greatly obstruct direct realisation, and what counters each?
options: craving and anger; countered by compassion
laziness and sleep; countered by vigour
objects and body; countered by retreat
disturbance by improper reflection, and a mind inverted about what should be known; mindfulness of breath for the first, the applications of mindfulness for the second
quiz.why: "First, disturbance caused by improper reflection, leaving the mind unsettled; second, a mind inverted regarding what should be known." "To counter the first obstruction, one cultivates mindfulness of the breath; to counter the second, the applications of mindfulness."

quiz.q: On entering direct realisation "the mind is free of alarm." What alarm is gone, per the two masters?
options: "where has my self gone?" — the dread of losing the self; on entering realisation one no longer worries about it
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "where, now, has my self gone?" is the mark of terror — "where am I now? I fear I no longer exist." Master Cháng Bǎi: the mind is no longer alarmed, no longer worried about where "my self" has gone.

quiz.q: What attainment does Venerable Miào Jìng say entering direct realisation is?
options: stream-entry — a partial realisation of nirvāṇa
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the state of direct realisation of the truths is that of stream-entry; when stream-entry appears, nirvāṇa is partially realised. Master Cháng Bǎi: through the sixteen moments of eight acceptances and eight knowledges, one attains stream-entry.
